subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Save More Tomorrow
description: A short lesson to help you apply Save More Tomorrow.

hook.text: Workers refuse to save more today. But ask them to save more starting next year and most say yes.

buildup.text: Thaler and Benartzi designed Save More Tomorrow: commit now to increase savings with each future raise.

discovery.text: Present bias makes current sacrifice painful. Linking future increases to future raises removes the pain because.

twist.text: Participants in the first trial increased savings from 3.5% to 13.6% over four years. Almost nobody dropped out.

climax.text: Save More Tomorrow is behavioral judo: it uses present bias and inertia, normally harmful forces, as engines.

punchline.text: Commit now for later. Your future self will thank your present self.

quiz.question: Why does Save More Tomorrow work?
options: It links future saving increases to future raises, avoiding felt loss

details.summary: Save More Tomorrow is a program where employees commit in advance to allocating a portion of future pay raises to retirement savings. By linking savings increases to future income rather than current income, it eliminates the loss aversion that blocks saving.
details.whyItMatters: Save More Tomorrow exploits three behavioral insights simultaneously: present bias by committing now for the future, loss aversion by avoiding decreases in take-home pay, and inertia by making increases automatic.
takeaways: Committing future raises to savings avoids feeling of income loss
Average savings rates rose from 3.5 to 13.6 percent over four auto-escalations
The program leverages present bias, loss aversion, and inertia simultaneously

faq.question: Why is Save More Tomorrow so effective?
faq.answer: It removes every behavioral barrier at once. Present bias is addressed by committing now. Loss aversion is addressed by only saving from future raises. Inertia is addressed by making escalation automatic. Each barrier is sidestepped rather than fought.

faq.question: Does Save More Tomorrow reduce participant happiness?
faq.answer: No. Because contributions only increase when income increases, take-home pay never decreases. Participants report no loss in lifestyle quality because their standard of living rises with each raise, just more slowly than without the program.
